title: Love Unveiled with A. H. Almaas

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for metamodern mutants interested in meditation, awakening, hardcore dharma, beauty, love, and much more. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the show. And in this episode, I'll be speaking once again with Hameed Ali. Hameed Ali, whose pen name is A. H. Almaas, is founder of the Diamond Approach to Self-Realization, a contemporary teaching that developed within the context of both ancient spiritual teachings and modern depth psychology theories. Almaas has authored 18 books about spiritual realization, including the Diamond Heart series, The Pearl Beyond Price, The Void, and The Alchemy of Freedom. And now, without further ado, I give you the episode that I call Love Unveiled with A. H. Almaas.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Hameed, welcome to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast for the second time.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Well, I'm happy to be here for the second time.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, our last talk was such a delight for me. And what a change, right? Last time we were in your office in Berkeley, you know, together looking at each other's faces and talking. And now in the time of COVID, even though we're, you know, in the same city, we're in our separate spaces talking over technology. And I'm just so aware of how different the situation is these days.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Well, the world has changed.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes, it sure has.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: The whole world, it's not just here. I mean, it's a big change. And we tried to do it, we were attempting to get face-to-face, but the COVID kept developing.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes. And how is that going for you? How are you feeling about the whole COVID situation currently?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: I'm personally okay. I am staying safe. I'm healthy and all my family are okay.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's very good news.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: You know, I don't like the fact that we have it. I wish we didn't. And, you know, there's a lot of people who are suffering and the economy is suffering. I mean, it's a big impact on all of the human race.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Very big. Are you finding that it's a major topic in your teaching or with your students currently?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: It's not a major one, but it comes up. Like, all of our teachings now are online, for instance.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, no in-person retreats.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Yeah, we used to do it always in person, and now we do everything online. So that's different. And, you know, of course, people ask questions about it, we discuss it. It's not the main thing that we would be teaching, our teaching, our work. But I try to make it sort of relevant to the times.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay, so the big thing on the agenda here is that you have a new book called Love Unveiled. And this is a very, very fascinating text. I was lucky enough, your helper there sent me an advance copy, so I got a chance to look through that. And it's just extremely fascinating. And I think a very, very relevant topic. And so how would you feel if we jumped right in and talked about some of the aspects that you're discussing in that book?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: That sounds good to me. Hopefully we'll get into some kind of depth and help our audience get some kind of taste.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That would be great. And of course, this is your topic. So as we're moving along, feel free to keep nudging it deeper and deeper into the deep end of this discussion.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: I would really like that.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: I'm glad we can go deep.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. So the initial thing I would say is that when we're talking about spirituality or meditation, and we're talking about consciousness or awareness, nonduality, it's very, very common, not always, but very common, that either people reduce the entirety of the practice to something about awareness, and it's sort of like, you know, pure, clear awareness, awareness itself, nothing but awareness, or that they say that awareness has facets, like maybe there's some compassion in there or some warmth together, you know, it has some facets or features. But it seems like you're saying that actually, no, that there is love and that is something that is quite different than simply awareness. And so am I understanding this correctly? And what can you say about that?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: You understand correctly. And it is one reason why I wrote the book, to bring in a perspective that is partly a corrective.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So please, correct our perspective here.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Well, because as you said, most people when they talk about spirituality these days, because of the dominance of the nondual view that comes from the East, the focus is on consciousness and awareness. In the Western world, if we look at the spirituality of the Western world, whether it's Christian mysticism or the Sufis, you know, which is the Islamic mysticism, the focus is more on love, in relationship to the divine, and love as the main thing. In fact, Rumi says, love is it. Love is reality. Love is God. He doesn't talk about awareness much. Doesn't mean he doesn't know about awareness, doesn't recognize awareness, but love is important. And, you know, the way I see it, the way it's corrective is that people need to know that their spiritual nature, it is true, it is pure consciousness, but it is also pure love, pure compassion, pure intelligence. All these things are inherent in our spiritual nature. Awareness is fundamental, but love is what speaks to human beings, and it's really what transforms human beings and what makes transformation easy for human beings, which is something not addressed by the people who focus on awareness or emptiness, for that matter.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, it seems like in our everyday concept of love, like love of our partner or love of our family or even love of God, people seem to be talking about something that is in some way a shadow or a lesser expression of love than what I think you're describing.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: You got it right here, Michael. And that is another corrective that the book does, or more informative and adding to our understanding of love, that what we experience emotionally as love is a reflection, a shadow of the real thing, which is more in the spirit level, which is pure presence, pure light. And so it is self-existent, it is on its own, it's not a reaction from our nervous system. It comes from the spiritual world, from our spiritual ground, and fills the heart and fills the consciousness and comes out in our generosity and affection and all that. So what people know as love is really an approximation to that, but more of a reflection, I think. And because it is not the real, true love, which is more of a spiritual presence, a spiritual kind of element, human love gets into possessiveness and reactivity and jealousy and things like that. It's self-centered. And I think that is one reason why the Eastern traditions tend to avoid talking about love, because they think love has to do with attachment.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: It brings an attachment, which it can, but that's more the usual human love that most people feel, which is more emotional. That brings an attachment. When we experience love on the essential level, on the spiritual level, experience it as presence, it is like part of what I am. It is part of my being. One way my being manifests is as the richness and the sweetness and generosity of love, but it is really fullness, richness of spirit, which appears as the heartfulness of realization, the heartfulness of a spiritual experience.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And how is that qualitatively different than, say, just the emotion of love, or that emotion of sweetness that anyone would recognize when they see their, let's say, favorite dog or something? You know, they feel that sweetness, they feel love. How is that different?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Well, I mean, people can say, well, you're so sweet, or you feel sweet. But do they really taste the sweetness? Or is it just an expression, a loving expression, meaning you say it's sweet? But when I talk about sweetness, I mean you really taste sweetness. You taste like sugar. You taste like honey. And the taste is in the heart, not on the tongue. So the whole consciousness becomes this sweetness, full of the sweetness. But the sweetness, as I'm saying, is not metaphorical. It's actually direct sensation and experience of a sweet kind of atmosphere, a sweet presence, that makes us feel love is delightful, delectable and yummy and pleasurable, and which makes us glow with a kind of generosity and selfless appreciativeness, not a possessive one.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And what would you say is the relationship between consciousness and love, if they're sort of on the same level? What is the relationship between them?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: You see, if we go to the nondual teachings, they will think that love is an expression of consciousness or awareness. And the teaching I myself teach, the Diamond Approach, I see both consciousness and awareness as expressions of spiritual nature. They are both expressions. Awareness, it happens to be there all the time, because we are conscious, aware people. But even when we are conscious, we're not really knowing the awareness of the consciousness, and its is-ness and its presence and its facticity. So we're just aware of the function of awareness. We're not aware of awareness itself. Awareness itself, it is a kind of clear, transparent medium. And love, it's the same way, it's a medium. But it is a sweet and beautiful golden or pink or some kind of medium, instead of colorless, the way awareness is. So the way I look at it, we can do it both from the nondual, or from a deeper level, what I consider a deeper level than nondual, which is an indefinable spiritual nature, which is the source of awareness and love, which can manifest as pure love, everything is love, or it manifests as awareness.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And we see everything is awareness or consciousness. That's clear. Would you also say that everything is love?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Yes, you can say the same thing. In fact, that's what Rumi and the Sufi poets talk about, that everything is love. And one thing I wanted to point to. When you look at spiritual teachers and masters, there are the ones who are illuminated and radiate clarity and selflessness and all of that. But there are also those who are radiating clarity and selflessness, but also have richness and juiciness to them. It shows that there is heart, that love is coming through with awareness. I'll give you examples. For instance, if you think of one of the nondual teachers, Ramana Maharshi. Ramana Maharshi, when you look at his picture, you see love. He talks about the Self or the ultimate, which is pure consciousness, but he exemplifies sweetness of love much more than any of the other nondual teachers of Advaita Vedanta. If you go to Dzogchen, also nondual, there are many Dzogchen teachers, but if you remember somebody like Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche. When you look at his face and his eyes, he's exuding sweetness and love and liking of others. He's not just aware. So I see love as a maturation of realization. Awareness is realization. To recognize your awareness, that you are aware, this is realization or liberation. The maturation of that realization will have to include love, where love will manifest as one way this awareness expresses itself, especially in human life.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And how do we learn to tell the difference between the clinging human level of love, with a lot of expectation and personal selfishness, and this deeper, open-hearted spiritual love?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Good question, Michael. Two ways. One of the ways is in the expression and the way we live it, or, you know, act it out in life. Emotional human love usually has a lot of drama around it. You fall in love, there's excitement, there is, you know, heartache, there is longing, there is rejection, fear, and if one is fulfilled, then there's possessiveness and jealousy. That's what happens, all of that. That shows in expression. And if you feel it inside, you might feel love, but you feel more like a desire and wanting, and with a lot of fantasy around it. When it comes to the spiritual or essential love, the expression of it, there's equanimity in it. There is a givingness and a good-hearted expression that is kind, that is sweet, that is loving, that is more one thing that functions to make the other person happy and feel good, and not wanting anything from them. So in the expression, in the behavior, there is no sign of possessiveness and wanting. It's just simply giving and generosity and happiness in the happiness of others. And if somebody is happy, you're just happy for them. If you love them, you're even more happy for them. In terms of the actual inner state, the difference from regular emotional love, and the regular emotional love, as I said, feels inside as a reaction, emotion, a desire and wanting, and an intense passion maybe, or some kind of a melting. And the spiritual love I'm talking about, you experience it as an inner medium that has texture. It's a fullness of presence. You feel it as a presence in the sense that when you feel it, you feel more here, more now, more present, more fully yourself. I feel more love fills me, I feel I am here because love is here, appearing as presence, as the very beingness of my consciousness, the very beingness of my spirit. But it is a medium, and when I say a medium, I feel the consciousness as a field. But the field here has a fullness, has a texture, has a taste, has a color. The color could be golden or pink or pomegranate, or a glowing color to it, and the sense of purity. But the sense of fullness is the texture, is like, as if your heart is full of nectar or dripping with honey. So that is almost a physical experience of love, but it is really not physical, because the presence feels like substance, but it is not really material substance. It's more the fullness of being, the fullness of the spiritual nature, but appearing in the quality of love. So that's a very big difference than emotional love. You don't feel that in emotional love. And also in the sense that inside it's not like a medium only necessarily filling the heart, it could expand, fill the whole room, fill the whole universe. You could feel the whole universe is full of the same medium, glowing and sweet, smooth texture, of a delightful kind of pleasurable happiness, and appreciate the light and the sight of reality, and the sight of the divine, and the sight of nature, and the sight of other people.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: As I listen to you talking, I'm reminded of the bhakta tradition in India and Radha-Krishna literature that is so beautifully rich with images of longing and desire and love. And it's fascinating because, of course, if we're coming from a nondual tradition, coming from particularly a Buddhist tradition, there's this sense that we should somehow stamp out desire or remove longing or flatten it or get it cut out surgically or something, like it's bad. In fact, you know, it's the ultimate thing in some traditions that we're trying to remove. And yet here's this whole other tradition, many traditions actually, as you said, the Sufi tradition and also the bhakta tradition, are actually focusing on desire or yearning as the most important thing. So how do you model the role of this longing, this yearning, this desire in spirituality?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Well, as you know, the spiritual search begins with a desire, with a yearning, and it becomes a seeking and search before we get into the awakening and enlightenment. And you wonder, where does this yearning and this desire come from? You know, when we inquire into the desire and yearning, which are utilized in the bhakti tradition, they are really the outer expression of love. We yearn for something because we want it. We want it because we love it. We like having it. We like being close to it. So love is at the very heart of desire and yearning. But on the ordinary level, when we experience love only as emotional response or a desire, wanting, we're feeling the outer expression of love. We're not feeling the love itself. Love itself doesn't have yearning. So the bhakti tradition, you see, when they talk about yearning and all of that and love, it's a mixture of the two levels. There is the yearning, the longing, and the desire mixed with the sweetness of love. So that makes the bhakti attitude. But the bhaktas, when they become realized, they just experience love, and then there's no desire, there's just celebration, enjoyment. Like when the Indian bhakta has a vision of Krishna, for instance, there's a sense of awe and celebration. The yearning got them there, but when they're there, it's the fullness, the effulgence of love.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I see what you're saying. So, of course, the desire or the yearning falls by the wayside at the end either way. I think it's so fascinating, though, that rather than kind of denying or suppressing desire, in these traditions we can follow it home, so to speak, or follow the yearning of the heart back to the center of love.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Yeah, many traditions do that, both East and West. And really, the way it appears in the nondual teachings is that the love is between the student and the guru. The student is to revere and love the guru, instead of in relation to the divine. So it's not like nondual teachings don't have bhakti. They do, but it is not seen as the method. And one thing, you know, I was remembering, have you heard of Atmananda, one of the main Advaita Vedanta masters?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Atmananda, who teaches basically nondual witnessing, which is mere recognition of consciousness, his followers in the U.S. now and in other places, that's all they teach in their satsang, how to recognize consciousness. But when you read the biography of Atmananda himself, when he met his guru, his guru gave him several things to practice. The first thing he had to practice for a long time was the bhakti. He had to practice bhakti yoga. So he began his training as a bhakta before he became a jnani, where he knows about consciousness. So in that tradition, really, the bhakti is very important, but the modern students don't do the bhakti part, although Atmananda practiced it himself before he got to the pure awareness.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes, and I'm thinking about how even in the tantric tradition, the Vajrayana tradition, one would do the ngöndro first, which would include quite a bit of devotion and love towards the teacher. And that's the preliminary step, right, before working with anything else.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Yeah, and when you look at the truly accomplished masters, like in the Buddhist tradition, if you look at Dilgo Khyentse, if you look at the Dalai Lama right now, the Dalai Lama, he's full of love and compassion and heart. Although he talks about emptiness and awareness, he also talks about love and compassion. And he is full of love and compassion. He's an embodiment of it. So that tradition is not empty of love and heart. It's just empty awareness is seen as the enlightenment, which makes sense. I mean, I have that experience and it's true from it. But you see, the trick is that the empty awareness is the enlightenment, but then the enlightenment needs to mature, and the maturation of that enlightenment is the arising of the heart, the fullness of the heart, as is seen in the case of the Dalai Lama or somebody like Dilgo Khyentse.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: How do you approach teaching this opening of the heart to your students?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: So the way I do it is direct. Meaning, first of all, since love is one way that our spiritual nature, which is our true nature, can express itself, manifest itself, if we're not aware of it, there must be some barriers, must be some obstacles in the way. Otherwise, how come it is part of being ourselves? So we first work on obstacles to it, which has to do with one's psychology, one's identity, one's sense of self, one's history. And because many people, you know, they don't experience love directly, because love is important for a human being, we need it when we're babies, love is what most people talk about. And a person who is not loved doesn't grow well, and the person who is really loved tends to grow better. And it's been actually researched and all of that, to find that that's true, not just for human beings, for mammals in general. So I work on the fact that if we have love within our nature, and it's something we really need, we really want, why don't we feel it directly? So we found what I call obstacles or barriers in the way. And this teaching I have is that depending on the quality of love, the kind of love, there are specific barriers that we can work with with students by doing practices and exercises and inquiring with the student into those barriers. And then, by seeing it, the historical origins, the barriers begin to sort of dissolve. And as they dissolve, then the space is open for the heart to reveal its love, its nature, loving nature.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: What would be an example of one of these barriers?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: For instance, if you take loving kindness, for instance, right, to feel kind and loving towards somebody's pain. One of the barriers here is that we don't want to feel our own wounding, our own emotional hurt. So if we allow ourselves to recognize that we don't want to feel our own emotional hurts, everybody got emotional wounding, because all the relationships where they had, not just with their parents, but later on with lovers or friends, deal with the wounding and they experience the wounding. The wounding itself will become an opening into that deeper level of heart where the juices of love will begin to arise from within the wound, actually. That's an example. Another kind of love is what I call the melting, the merging love, when it makes us feel we want to be close to, connected with somebody. We want to be so much unified with them, with the situation. That has to do with our original relationship with our mother, where that kind of very deep connection is what happens between the infant and the mother. So difficulties in that first relationship will appear as difficulties in having access to this quality of love. So we deal with those old distortions or difficulties or problematic relationships earlier on by first reliving it emotionally, understanding it, and as it dissolves, it makes it possible for us to experience this quality. And then we feel the sweetness of a golden kind of love, the consciousness that makes us feel some kind of nourishing kind of presence, just the way an infant who is with a loving mother would feel. But now we are not an infant, we are the presence itself. Another quality, for instance, is appreciative love, which is when you say you like somebody, you appreciate them, you know and want to know about them as much as possible. That's a different kind of love, and the issue in it is the fact that we feel not loved. If we were not loved, our love was limited or conditional. So, just everybody is different, seeing how we feel rejected, not loved or not loved enough, and how that makes us feel. So all these are emotional things, what we call the knots of the heart. Rumi will call them the knots of the heart, or the windings of the bosom, he will call them. So working with these, you know, and inquiring into them, and feeling them, and by feeling them, getting insight about what they're about and how they are impressions from the past. They don't have to be here anymore. And if you understand, they tend to dissolve. And as they dissolve, the heart has a spaciousness, an openness, within which the particular quality of love will begin to arise.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And if you were to point someone towards having an experience, a deeper experience of love or a more complete opening of love, how would you point that out? What's your way into the heart?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Well, I mean, you can do it as a kind of a guided meditation, which I do sometimes, which is taking one from the usual experience of love and letting them feel how it speaks of something deeper, and to feel into their heart and see where it's coming from. What is it a reflection of? They might begin to experience the real thing that gets reflected in the usual experience of love. And also, frequently somebody will tell me, I feel grateful. I'll tell them, well, what's that feel like? And they say, oh, I feel like I'm really happy with what I said. Yeah, that's what you tell me. But when you feel in your heart, what do you experience? And that's when they begin to say, oh, it feels like there is a nectar. That will be the recognition on their part.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And can you describe anything about this nectar?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Well, there are many kinds of nectar, as I mentioned. I mentioned different kinds. But remember, the heart, first of all, has many qualities, and it's all sort of the nature of love, but the heart has things like fulfillment, has something like gratitude, you know. So, and people don't think of these as love, but they are qualities of the heart. They have similar thing to what love has, which is, and they are all nectars. And a kind of love is the passionate love, for instance. Passionate love is zesty, is passionate, is ecstatic, but it feels like a strong feeling and a tart kind of nectar. And if you taste it, it tastes like pomegranate juice, actually, almost like pomegranate syrup. And you can see it, it looks like pomegranate, if you see it. But the feeling of it is a love that has power, that has passion, that has intensity, that has an ecstasy, that kind of pleasure. So that's a kind of nectar. It looks like pomegranate syrup. The other kind, like the merging, the melting and wanting to be together and wanting to be sort of not separate, all of that, this appears like a golden nectar, like honey with the sun shining through it. The texture and the density is not as dense as honey, not as sticky as honey, but it is a beautiful, delicate kind of a glowing golden nectar that fills the heart, seeps through the consciousness, melts the tensions, melts the obstacles. Many people talk about love. Like even Rumi talks about love all the time. He never described what it feels like. What is the inner experience of it? How do you feel it? They say sweet, but sweet what? So even the teachings of love, they don't go into the phenomenology of it. So in this book, I'm trying to bring out the phenomenology of love. What is the physiognomy? What kind of consciousness? When it is felt, what does it feel like? How does it impact the body and mind? Something like that. So that's what I'm trying to bring out. It's not just love and good and selfless and giving. All that's true, but that doesn't say yet the phenomenology, that it is like a nectary kind of consciousness, conscious of itself as sweet nectar.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And for you, how has this been arising? Like, is it a recent opening in your own experience or is it something that was there from early on?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Depends what you mean by recent. I'm in my seventies. Well, I had some of that in my early childhood, but I wasn't aware of them by the time I started practicing in my late 20s. So as my spiritual openings started happening, it included those qualities of love in late 20s, and beginning in 30s I was experiencing these things and understanding them. That is when the teaching that we call the Diamond Approach was beginning to formulate itself. These are things I've been experiencing for decades. These fill my life, fill my relationships.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And currently, what for you is kind of the interaction or the relationship between the awakened consciousness or awakened mind and the awakened heart? How do they intermingle or interact?

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: Now, one way of saying it is using, you know, a Gurdjieff way of looking at things, that a human being is a three-brained being, the belly, the heart and the head. So the head has to do with illumination, with enlightenment, with awareness. The heart has to do with love, with goodness. And the belly has to do with the solidity of being, of presence. So these are all different dimensions of the same nature. There's different qualities, facets of the same nature. So in my teaching, love is necessary to approach truth, because my approach is all predicated on loving the truth for its own sake. I love to find out what is the truth of my experience, the truth of reality, your truth, truth of anything. So love is already the motive power for the practice. And then the truth we discover, some of the truth is first presence, and then presence appears as nature of our awareness, that makes us discover awareness and consciousness. Then that consciousness matures, and part of its maturation is the fullness of heart as love.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Why is it that so many people seem to have a difficulty feeling loved by the world, by others, or feeling even love for themselves? These would seem to be kind of fundamental, important attributes, and yet so many people report having a very difficult time with this.

transcript.speaker: A. H. Almaas
transcript.text: It's the story of the human race. Human beings, just like mammals, but human beings more, need lots of love, especially at the beginning. And human life is informed by love. When you talk with your friends, with people, in most of the movies and the stories, it's all about love, love relationship. People don't talk about awareness or emptiness, whatever, in their daily discourse. Whether somebody loves them, whether they love somebody, whether they're in love or not, fallen out of love or not, or they're hurt because of love, it's all about love. And so the result is that love is important, but our environment, our society, has not developed to the point of view where love is that easily accessible, easily present. So most people, their parents are not that loving, or they didn't love them enough, or they loved them, then they loved somebody else, they felt abandoned. And so abandonment, limitation of early love, rejection, it creates wounds in the heart. And we get wounded, people get wounded, and the wounding becomes then suppressed, because it's painful to feel. And then from the wounding there is anger for being hurt and rejected or not wanted and all of that, anger and hatred. All those are the emotions that result mostly around love, really. Love, the original feeling, let's put it this way, the original primordial affect of the heart is love. Everything else bifurcates from there. It's either an expression of it, or a distortion of it, or reaction to it. And that is mostly the human suffering. What we call human suffering is mostly of the heart, more than anything else. Buddhism talks about the mind, but what do they mean by the mind? They don't really mean just thinking. They mean the totality of consciousness, which includes the heart. Most of human suffering is really emotional suffering, as you know. True, people worry and think and all that, and especially if you meditate, you recognize how your thoughts are a problem.
